title: Pe Hebrew Letter (פ): Pe, Fe & Final Pe
description: Learn the Hebrew letter Pe (פ), also spelled Pey: its [p] sound with a dagesh, its [f] sound (Fe), final Pe (ף), words like פֶּה (mouth) and practice.

5.label: Fey (Pey without Dagesh)
5.equivalent: Pey without a dot (dagesh) in its center, pronounced [f]. This form is called Fey.

8.label: Pey with Dagesh
8.equivalent: Pey with a dot (dagesh) in its center, pronounced [p]. Without the dot, it is pronounced [f].

12.label: Fey Sofit
12.equivalent: Final Pey: Pey with its stroke extended below the line, written at the end of a word and pronounced [f].

blocks.0: Pe Hebrew Letter (פ): Pe, Fe, Final Pe & Practice
blocks.7: The Hebrew word 'שָׂפָה' [sa-fa] means 'language'. The first letter is Sin (שׂ), with a dot on the upper left, giving [s]. Its Kamatz Gadol gives [a], making [sa]. Pey (פ) without a dagesh gives [f], and its Kamatz Gadol gives [a], making [fa]. Hey (ה) at the end of the word is silent here. Say two syllables, sa-fa, with the stress on fa.
blocks.16: The Hebrew word 'פֶּה' [pe] means 'mouth'. It has two letters: Pey (פּ) and Hey (ה). The dagesh gives Pey its [p] sound, and the Segol (ֶ) beneath it gives [e]. Hey at the end of the word is silent here. Say pe as one syllable.
blocks.18: The Hebrew word 'יָפָה' [ya-fa] means 'beautiful' in the feminine singular, used with a feminine singular noun or to describe a woman or girl. It has three letters: Yud (י), Pey (פ), and Hey (ה). Yud gives [y], as in 'yes', and its Kamatz Gadol gives [a], making [ya]. Pey has no dagesh, so it gives [f]; its Kamatz Gadol gives [a], making [fa]. Hey at the end of the word is silent here. Say two syllables, ya-fa, with the stress on fa.

1.tip: Both represent [f]; ף is the final form. Pey with a dagesh (פּ) represents [p].

4.tip: Fey Sofit (ף) represents [f] and is used at the end of words, as in אַף [af], 'nose'.

5.content: How is the letter Fey Sofit (ף) pronounced?
5.tip: Fey Sofit (ף) is pronounced the same as Fey (פ) – as [ f ].

7.tip: Pey (פּ) with a dagesh has a hard [ p ] sound.

9.tip: Kamatz Gadol represents [a], roughly as in 'father'. With Pey (פּ), it makes [pa]; no special vowel length is required.

10.tip: In most cases, Hey (ה) at the end of a word is silent.

15.tip: Both represent [f]. Adding a dagesh to the regular form gives פּ, pronounced [p].

theory.heading: Meet Pe
theory.intro: The seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Pe, also spelled Pey (the spelling used in this lesson), can make two sounds: with a dot inside (a dagesh) it is [p], as in “pot”; without the dot it is [f], as in “fun,” and is often called Fe (Fey). Pe is also one of the five letters with a final form: at the end of a word it is written ף, final Pe (called Fey Sofit here), usually pronounced [f].
objectives: Recognize Pe: <bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">פ</bdi>, and its final form, <bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">ף</bdi>.
Tell Pe with a dagesh (<bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">פּ</bdi>, [p]) apart from Pe without one (<bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">פ</bdi>, [f]).
Read both sounds in real words like <bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">פֶּה</bdi> (mouth) and <bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">יָפָה</bdi> (beautiful).

examples.heading: Pe, Fe and final Pe in real words
examples.intro: See how the dagesh changes the sound of Pe and how final Pe is written, then read three words aloud.
